title: How to Play
intro: Everything below describes the rules as the game actually implements them today. Numbers come straight from the shared match and deck configuration, so they are always the ones your match will use. Where a rule has deliberately not been decided yet, this book says so rather than inventing an answer.

blocks.text: You and up to three opponents each command a deck and one Commander. The last player still standing wins. There are no teams: everyone plays for themselves.
How a player loses

items: Their health drops to zero or below.
They have to draw a card and their deck is empty.
They concede.
They disconnect and do not return within {matchConfig.disconnectGraceSeconds} seconds.

blocks.text: Losing conditions are checked after every single instruction an effect carries out, and again after combat damage is dealt. If the last remaining players all lose in the same check, the match is a draw.

blocks.title: Losing your Commander is not losing the match
blocks.text: A Commander that is defeated on the battlefield goes back to your Command Zone and can be deployed again. There is no Commander-damage clock and no Commander-defeat loss condition.

items: One player creates a lobby and shares its six-character invite code. A lobby seats {matchConfig.minPlayers} to {matchConfig.maxPlayers} players.

Everyone joins and submits a deck: either a built-in precon, picked by name and played exactly as it comes, or one of their own saved decks. The server validates every deck against the pool of the format being played and rejects illegal ones with reasons.
Everyone marks ready. The seat order and the starting player are rolled from the match seed.
Each player draws their opening hand.
Each player decides, privately, whether to keep it. Nobody sees anyone else's decision until all of them are in.
The first turn begins.

blocks.text: The opening hand

To redraw, choose any number of cards from your opening hand and return them. You immediately draw the same number, and only then are the returned cards shuffled back into your deck — so you can never draw one of them straight back.

blocks.title: The first player skips a draw
blocks.text: Going first is an advantage, so the player who takes the first turn skips their very first draw step. Everyone else draws normally from their first turn onwards.
A deck is exactly one Commander plus a fixed number of other cards. The Commander is not part of the deck: it starts in the Command Zone, is never shuffled in and is never drawn.

blocks.title: You do not have to build one
blocks.text: Every built-in precon can be played as it comes: pick it by name in the lobby's deck list and the match server plays the printed list. Copy it in the deck builder instead if you want to change it — an edited copy is your own deck, and is checked like any other.

blocks.label: One copy of each card only

blocks.text: Copies

In a singleton format no card may appear in your deck twice, however the deck was written down. Splitting a card across two entries of one copy each does not get past it: the rule is about the card, not about the line it is written on. The copy limits below still apply, and in a singleton format they are both one.
Colour identity

Your Commander has one or more colours. A card is legal in your deck only if every colour in its identity also appears in your Commander's identity. Neutral cards have no colours at all and are legal under any Commander.
Which cards you may pick from

items: The pool is the format's own pool, not every card that exists. A card belonging to another format is not offered and is refused if a saved deck still holds one.
A card that is still being built is refused by name, and so is a Commander that is still being built. An unfinished card is never quietly played as a blank.
The deck builder checks all of this live, and the server checks it again against the same rules before the match starts. Its verdict is the one that counts.
Name — what the card is called. Names can change; the card's internal identity never does, so decks and replays never break.
Cost — energy you pay to play it. A Commander's printed cost is what you pay to deploy it out of the Command Zone. Tokens are never paid for and show no cost.
Type — unit, spell, reaction, relic, Commander or token.
Colours — the coloured bar. It decides which Commanders can run the card.
Attack and health — units, Commanders and tokens only. Attack is damage dealt; health is damage survived.
Keywords — named rules shorthand, listed as chips. Every keyword is defined in this book.
Rules text — what the card does, written out. It is a description of the card's structured effects, never the thing that makes them happen.
Artwork — decoration. A card with no artwork uses a default image and plays exactly the same.

blocks.title: Text never drives behaviour
blocks.text: Card behaviour comes from structured data the rules engine executes. The sentence you read is generated from, or checked against, that data — so a card can never do something its text does not describe because someone edited the wrong field. In a match you can open any visible card in Help mode to see its effects explained step by step, in the order they resolve.

items: Unit — goes onto your battlefield and stays there. It can attack and block. It resolves its own effects as it arrives.
Spell — resolves its effects immediately, then goes to your discard pile. It never stays in play.
Reaction — played from your hand only inside an open Reaction window, which can happen on anybody's turn. It resolves and then goes to your discard pile, like a spell.
Relic — goes into a separate row and stays until something removes it or another relic replaces it. Relics are not units and cannot attack or block.
Commander — starts in the Command Zone rather than in your deck, and can be deployed to the battlefield for its printed cost.
Token — a unit created by an effect. Tokens are never in a deck, and a token that leaves play stops existing entirely.

blocks.text: Where cards go

Every card is in exactly one place: your deck, your hand, the battlefield, your discard pile, the Command Zone, or out of the game. A card that changes place arrives as a fresh copy of itself — damage marked on it, bonuses given to it and anything else that had been done to it are all left behind.

items: The discard pile is public and is not the end of the road. A card can come back from it, and a few cards bring one back.

A card put onto the battlefield from the discard pile has not been deployed: nobody paid its cost. It is Newly Deployed, so it cannot attack or pay an Exhaust cost until your next Ready Step, and it can arrive Exhausted if the card that returned it says so.
Abilities that watch for a Unit entering the battlefield see a returned Unit. Abilities that watch for a Unit being deployed do not.
A card removed from the game is gone for good. It is not in any pile, nothing may target it, and no effect returns it. You can still see how many cards each player has had removed.

blocks.title: There is no limit on units
blocks.text: You can have as many units on your battlefield as you can afford to play. Nothing is refused for lack of room, and a token that an effect creates is always created. Energy is the only thing that limits how fast a board grows.
Energy is the only resource. There are no resource cards to draw and nothing to miss: your maximum simply grows on its own, every one of your turns.

blocks.label: Maximum energy on your first turn
Maximum energy gained each of your turns

blocks.text: Energy you did not spend

Unspent energy is not lost at the end of your turn. It stays with you through everybody else's turns, and it is what pays for a Reaction played on an opponent's turn. At the start of your own next turn your maximum rises and your energy is then set to that maximum — the refill replaces what you were holding rather than adding to it, so saving energy can never take you above your maximum.
Paying
Costs are paid in full before a card or ability starts resolving. If paying would be impossible, the action is refused outright and nothing is spent — you can never be left half-committed.

Some cards charge more than energy: sacrificing a unit, discarding a card, exhausting the source. You pay that as you play the card, before anyone can answer it, and you do not get it back if the card is countered. When such a cost lets you choose which unit to give up, the game asks you before anything at all is spent, and your answer is checked again against the board as it stands when you give it.
Costs that change

A card can cost less than the number printed on it. Some cards in your hand carry their own discount — “this card costs 1 less for each friendly Unit defeated this turn” — and others are made cheaper by something you control. Either way the discount is never written onto the card: it is worked out again every time the cost is asked for, so the number shown on the card in your hand is what you would pay right now, and it moves as the board moves.

A discount that prints “to a minimum cost of N” stops there. That floor never works in reverse: a card that already costs less than N is not pushed up to it. A discount with no printed floor really can take a card all the way to nothing.
Players take complete turns one at a time, in a fixed circle decided when the match is created. Each turn runs through the same phases in the same order.
You pass each Main Phase explicitly, and confirm your attackers and blockers explicitly. Assign Blockers is skipped entirely when nobody declared an attack.

blocks.title: Opponents act only inside named windows
blocks.text: There is no stack and no free-floating priority. On somebody else's turn you cannot play units, spells or relics, and you cannot use activated abilities. Two things can still happen: you assign blockers when you are attacked, and you play a Reaction inside one of the bounded windows the turn opens around combat and around spells. A Reaction window is an interruption rather than a phase of the turn, which is why it is not in the list above.
The Ready Step, and effects that stop it

At the start of your turn every permanent you control readies, and Newly Deployed clears. Some cards interfere with that step, and they do it in one of two ways. A card may fix a lock onto one permanent in advance — "it does not Ready during its controller’s next Ready Step" — which stays on that permanent even after the card that applied it has gone, and is used up by that one Ready Step whether or not there was anything to stop. Or a card already on the battlefield may offer, at the moment your permanents would ready, to keep one of them Exhausted for a price its controller pays.

Locks already in place are applied first, so nobody is ever asked to pay for a permanent that was going to stay Exhausted anyway. Only the Ready Step is affected: an effect that says "Ready target Unit" still readies a locked permanent, and Newly Deployed clears either way.

blocks.title: A replacement happens instead of the thing, not after it
blocks.text: "The first enemy Unit deployed each turn enters Exhausted" does not exhaust the unit once it is on the battlefield — the unit arrives Exhausted, and there is no moment in between for a trigger, a Reaction or another player to see it Ready. The same is true of a Token that arrives with a keyword. The log always names the card that did it.

During either of your Main Phases, with nothing currently resolving and no choice pending, you may play units, spells and relics, deploy your Commander, and use activated abilities, in any order you can pay for.
Units

items: A unit needs only its energy cost: your battlefield has no size limit.
It arrives ready, but Newly Deployed: it cannot attack, and cannot pay an "Exhaust this unit" cost, unless it has Rush.
It can block on the turn it arrives. Newly Deployed stops attacking, not blocking.
Newly Deployed lasts until your own next Turn Start, so it is still on the unit throughout your opponents' turns.
Its own effects resolve as it enters play.

blocks.text: Spells

items: A spell resolves its effects in the order they are written, then goes to your discard pile.
A spell that requires a target cannot be played at all when no legal target exists — it will not even be offered.
Playing a spell can open a Reaction window for your opponents. The spell waits until that window has been answered, so it can be countered before it does anything.

blocks.text: Relics

items: A relic goes into its own row and stays there until something removes it.
You may control {matchConfig.relicSlots} at a time. Playing another does not fail — it replaces the one you have.
The replaced relic goes to your discard pile as a rules action. It is not destroyed and not sacrificed, so nothing that watches for a relic dying will fire.

blocks.text: Your Commander

items: Deploying your Commander happens in your Main Phase like any other play, and costs its printed cost plus whatever its defeats have added.
Once deployed it is a unit in every way that matters, and it arrives Newly Deployed just as a unit does.
It is explained in full under "Your Commander".

blocks.text: Activated abilities

items: Only during your own Main Phase, and only when nothing else is resolving.
Costs may include energy, exhausting the card, discarding, or sacrificing a unit. All costs are paid together, before the ability starts.

An ability works only in the zone it is printed for. A Command Zone ability stops working once the Commander is deployed, and a battlefield ability does nothing while the Commander is still in the Command Zone.
A Newly Deployed source cannot pay an "Exhaust this unit" cost unless it has Rush. Other costs are unaffected.
Each ability states how often it may be used: once per match, once per turn, or as often as you can pay.

blocks.text: A Reaction is the only card you can play when it is not your turn. It is played from your hand, and only while a Reaction window that its printed timing admits is open.
When a window opens

items: After attackers are declared, and before blockers are assigned. These are the same moment, so one window serves both.
After blockers are assigned, and before combat damage — the last chance to change a combat.
After combat damage has been dealt and its defeats have settled.
When a player plays a spell. That spell waits in the window and resolves only once the window has finished.

blocks.text: A window opens only if somebody could actually use it. If nobody holds a Reaction whose timing fits and whose cost they can pay, the turn simply carries on, exactly as it would in a match with no Reactions in it at all.
How a window runs

items: Priority is offered to the active player first, then clockwise. It is only ever offered to a player who has something they could legally play.
You may play at most {matchConfig.reactionsPerPlayerPerWindow} Reaction in one window. Once you have played, you are finished for that window.
Priority goes round the table once. Playing a Reaction does not start the round again, so a player who has already declined is not asked a second time — decline and you have declined for that window.

Two different players can still each spend their one Reaction in the same window, and the second one resolves first. What you cannot do is wait to see what somebody else plays after you have already passed.
The window closes as soon as there is nobody left to offer it to.
Reactions are paid for out of the energy you carried over from your own turn.
You cannot respond to a Reaction that is already resolving. Nothing is interruptible once it has started.

blocks.text: How a window resolves

items: The cards resolve last in, first out: the Reaction played most recently resolves first.
The spell a window was opened around sits at the bottom, so it resolves last and can be countered by anything played above it.
A countered card goes to its owner's discard pile without doing anything. Its cost is not refunded.
Once everything has resolved, the turn carries on from exactly where it paused.

blocks.text: Declaring attackers

items: Choose any of your ready units that are not Newly Deployed. A unit with Rush may attack on the turn it arrives.
Your Commander attacks under exactly the same rules once it has been deployed.
Each attacker independently picks one living opponent to attack. Different attackers may attack different opponents.
Units attack players, never other units.
Every declared attacker exhausts immediately, whether or not it is blocked.
You can change your mind about any attacker right up until you confirm.

blocks.text: Declaring blockers

items: Only the player being attacked may block, and only against attacks aimed at them. You cannot block to protect somebody else.
A blocker must be ready. Blocking exhausts it, so a unit that attacked on your turn cannot block on the next one, and a blocker stays exhausted until your own turn starts.
A Newly Deployed unit may still block. That state stops attacking, not blocking.
One blocker per attacker, and each blocker blocks at most one attacker.
Attackers with Evasive cannot be blocked at all.
Guardian makes blocking compulsory. If you control ready Guardians, you must block at least as many of the attacks aimed at you as you have ready Guardians — or all of them, if fewer were declared.

You still choose which of your units do the blocking; it does not have to be the Guardians themselves. Attackers you could not legally block anyway, such as Evasive ones, do not count towards the obligation.
When several players are attacked at once, each answers separately and nobody sees anyone else's blocks until every defender has submitted.

blocks.text: Resolving combat

items: An unblocked attacker deals its attack as damage to the player it attacked.
A blocked attacker and its blocker deal damage to each other at the same time.
Units with Quick Strike deal their damage in an earlier step. Anything defeated in that step never strikes back.
Excess damage from a blocked attacker does not spill over to the defending player, unless the attacker has Overwhelm.

Overwhelm splits the damage: the blocker is assigned damage equal to its current health, and whatever is left over is dealt to the defending player. Damage already marked on the blocker does not increase the overflow.
Barrier on the blocker prevents only the share assigned to the blocker. The overflow that Overwhelm sent to the player is a separate hit and still lands.
If a blocker leaves play before damage, the attacker stays blocked and still deals no damage to the player.
Attack below zero counts as zero damage.

blocks.title: Reactions can change a combat
blocks.text: Windows open after attackers are declared, after blockers are assigned, and once combat damage has settled. See the Reactions section for how they run.
Damage dealt to a unit is marked on it and stays there across turns until something heals it. A unit is defeated as soon as its marked damage reaches its current health.

Defeats are never resolved one at a time in the middle of something. After each instruction, and after combat damage, the game runs a single check that defeats everything lethally damaged simultaneously — which is how two units can trade and both die.
Healing

items: Healing a unit removes marked damage and nothing else. It can never take a unit above its current health.
Healing a player raises their health, with no maximum.

blocks.text: Players and Commanders are separate

items: Card text that damages or heals a Commander means that player's own health total. It works whether or not any Commander has been deployed.
A Commander standing on the battlefield has its own health, tracked like any other unit's. Combat damage, and effects that target a unit, go there.
The two pools never touch. Damaging a player does nothing to their deployed Commander, and damaging a deployed Commander does nothing to its controller.

blocks.text: A defeated Commander

items: It returns to its owner's Command Zone immediately rather than going to the discard pile, and it can be deployed again.
Its defeat count goes up by one, and deploying it costs {matchConfig.commanderCostPerDefeat} more energy for each defeat, up to a total of {matchConfig.commanderCostCap}.
That is the whole of it. There is no recovery timer, no separate recovery zone and no loss condition attached.

blocks.text: Losing health bonuses
A temporary bonus that expires at end of turn takes its health back with it. A unit that survived only because of that bonus is defeated in the next check.
Elimination

items: An eliminated player's cards and tokens all leave the match. Tokens stop existing; other cards go to a removed pile.
Cards they controlled but did not own go back to their owner.
Attacks aimed at them are cancelled. The attackers stay exhausted and do not pick a new victim.
Choices they still owed are cancelled, and their queued effects end. They drop out of any open Reaction window, and the Reactions they had played there go with them.
All of that cleanup happens first, and only then does the game run one check and look for triggers.

blocks.text: Your Commander starts in the Command Zone, outside your deck. It is never shuffled in and never drawn, and its colour identity decides which cards are legal in your deck.
Deploying it

items: In either of your Main Phases you may deploy your Commander by paying its cost, exactly as you would play a unit out of your hand.
On the battlefield it behaves as a unit for readying, attacking, blocking, targeting, damage and Exhaust costs.
It arrives Newly Deployed, so it cannot attack on the turn you deploy it unless it has Rush. It can block straight away.
A Commander with no printed cost cannot be deployed at all. It stays in the Command Zone, and its abilities work from there.

blocks.text: Defeat and the cost tax

items: A defeated Commander returns to your Command Zone immediately. It is never gone for good, and it does not go to your discard pile.
Every defeat adds {matchConfig.commanderCostPerDefeat} energy to what deploying it costs from then on.
The tax is capped on the total, not on the surcharge: however many times your Commander falls, deploying it never costs more than {matchConfig.commanderCostCap} energy.
Losing your Commander costs you nothing else. There is no timer to wait out and no health penalty.

blocks.label: Highest a Commander's deployment cost can reach

blocks.text: Abilities and where they work

items: Every Commander ability names the zone it works in, and works only there.
A Command Zone ability stops the moment the Commander is deployed; a battlefield ability does nothing while the Commander is waiting in the Command Zone.
That is a property of each ability rather than of the card, so one Commander can carry both kinds.

blocks.title: "Damage to your Commander" means damage to you
blocks.text: Card text that deals damage to, or restores health to, a Commander is talking about that player's own health total, whether or not any Commander is on the battlefield. A deployed Commander's printed health is a separate pool, reached through combat or through an effect that targets a unit.
A larger table is a genuine free-for-all, not several duels running side by side. Every player competes independently and there are no teams.

items: Turns pass around a fixed circle. Eliminated seats are skipped and the circle is never renumbered.
Each of your attackers picks its own victim, so you can split an attack across two or three opponents in the same combat.
Only the player being attacked chooses blockers, and only for the attacks aimed at them.
An effect that says 'an opponent' asks you which one, when there is more than one to choose from.
An effect that says 'each opponent' works its way clockwise from you, and counts as happening all at once when it matters.
When several abilities trigger at the same moment, the active player's resolve first, then the rest clockwise. Nobody chooses the order.
A Reaction window offers priority to the active player first and then clockwise, and only ever to a player who could actually use it.
Once you are out, you keep watching but cannot act. You only ever see public information.

sections.title: Targets, choices and how effects resolve

blocks.text: Effects resolve through one first-in, first-out queue. There is no stack and no priority, so nothing can be responded to while it is resolving. The one place cards resolve out of order is inside a Reaction window, which drains last in, first out.
Order of events

items: You act. The server validates the action, the phase, the targets and the cost.
Costs are paid, and the effects join the queue.
Each instruction resolves in the order it is written on the card.
After each instruction the game checks for defeats and losses, then looks for abilities that have triggered.
New triggers wait until the current card has finished all of its own instructions, then join the queue behind whatever is already in it.

blocks.text: When you have to choose

items: An effect that needs a decision stops the whole queue until the right player answers. Nobody else can act in the meantime.
The legal options are worked out by the server. The client only shows them.
You are never asked a question with only one possible answer. A step with nothing to act on is skipped instead of being offered.

A step a card says you "may" take is offered as a yes or no. Saying no skips that step alone, and a later step that only happens "if you do" reads whether the step before it actually changed anything.
If a chosen target is no longer legal when the effect actually resolves, it is skipped and everything else still happens.
Searching a hidden zone such as your deck may legally find nothing. Searching a public zone must take a card if a legal one is there.

blocks.text: When everybody chooses at once

A few cards say "each player chooses". You are all making the same decision, so you are all asked before any of it happens: the answers are collected first and only then carried out. Nobody gets to see what anyone else picked before picking, and nobody's board changes while somebody else is still deciding.

items: You are asked in turn order, starting with the player whose card it is and going clockwise. That order also decides the order the answers are carried out in.
"A Unit they control" is read from each player's own side of the table: you choose from your units, each opponent chooses from theirs.
A player with no legal option is not asked at all, and everybody else still answers.
A player knocked out before the last answer arrives takes their choice with them.
An answer that has stopped being legal by the time the card resolves is dropped, and the rest still happens.

blocks.text: Splitting damage

When a card gives you damage to divide, the number is a total rather than an amount for each target. You allocate every point yourself, and you may put them all on one target. Each target then takes its whole share as a single hit — three points allocated to one unit is one hit of three, so Barrier stops that share once rather than once per point. Points with nowhere legal to go are simply lost.
Effects that happen later in the turn

Some cards promise something for later in the same turn rather than doing it now — "return it to your hand at the end of the turn", or "when it is defeated this turn, create two Tokens". The promise is set up the moment that instruction resolves, and everyone can see it waiting.

items: The card the promise is about is decided when it is set up, and is never chosen again. If the card the clause named moves to a different zone before the promise comes due, the promise is dropped — it was about the card where it was, not about wherever the card is now.
A promise that waits for an event only waits until the end of that turn. If the event never happens, nothing happens.
A promise never survives the turn it was made on, so nothing can carry over into somebody else's turn.
Promises made by a player who is eliminated end with them, exactly like their queued effects.

blocks.title: Runaway loops end safely
blocks.text: The engine counts resolution steps and watches for repeated states. A combination that would loop forever stops with a diagnostic instead of hanging the match.
Keywords are shorthand for rules that appear on many cards. Every keyword below is defined by what the rules engine actually does with it.
The words the rules themselves are written in.

blocks.title: You are going first in a two-player match
steps: Turn Start: your maximum energy becomes {matchConfig.startingMaxEnergy} and your energy is set to it. Nothing is exhausted yet.
Draw: you skip it, because you are the player going first.
Main Phase: you have {matchConfig.startingMaxEnergy} energy, so you play a one-cost unit onto your battlefield. It arrives Newly Deployed.
Declare Attackers: your only unit is Newly Deployed, so you confirm with nobody attacking.
Assign Blockers is skipped, because there were no attacks.
Second Main Phase: you have no energy left, so you pass.
Turn End: your hand is under the limit, so nothing is discarded. Play passes to your opponent, who draws normally on their turn.

blocks.title: Your second turn
steps: Turn Start: your unit readies, it stops being Newly Deployed, your maximum energy rises and your energy is set to that maximum.
Main Phase: you spend energy on a second unit.
Declare Attackers: your first unit is no longer Newly Deployed, so you attack with it. It exhausts as you declare.
Assign Blockers: your opponent may block with one of their units, or take the damage.
Resolve Combat: damage is dealt at the same time, and anything lethally damaged is defeated together.
Turn End: any energy you did not spend stays with you, and can pay for a Reaction on your opponent's turn.

items: Empty deck: drawing from an empty deck loses you the match. A multi-card draw resolves one card at a time, so you can lose part-way through it.
Hand limit: at the end of your turn you must discard down to the maximum hand size, choosing which cards to lose.
A very large board: there is no unit limit, so a token an effect creates is always created and nothing is ever destroyed to make room.
No legal target: a spell that needs a target and has none cannot be played. If a target becomes illegal later, it is skipped and the rest of the effect still resolves.
Blocker removed before damage: the attacker stays blocked and deals no damage to the player.
Expiring buffs: when a temporary health bonus ends, a unit whose marked damage now reaches its health is defeated straight away.
Sacrifice: a sacrificed unit counts as defeated as well, so both kinds of ability trigger.
A sacrificed Commander: sacrifice, destruction and lethal damage all send it back to the Command Zone and all raise its cost. There is no route that puts it anywhere else.
A countered card: the energy and any additional cost you paid for it are gone. Countering never refunds anything.
Nobody can answer: a Reaction window that nobody could legally act in never opens, and the turn does not pause.
Disconnecting: you have {matchConfig.disconnectGraceSeconds} seconds to come back. Refreshing the page reclaims your seat. At a larger table, everyone else carries on without you.

blocks.label: Maximum hand size at end of turn

blocks.title: Rules still being decided
blocks.text: Every number in this book is a playtest setting rather than a final decision. One keyword, Resilient, is printed on cards but does nothing yet, and its entry in the keyword list says so. The Reaction window policy — one Reaction each, active player first, one round of priority, last in first out — is deliberately the smallest workable rule and may be replaced. Nothing in this book describes a rule the game does not actually implement.
